div.head: Northu 2.3
div.ab: ⁊ ælc preost finde him XII festermen, þæt he preostlage wille healdan mid rihte.
And ælc preost finde him XII festermen, þæt he preostlage wille healdan mid rihte.
Und jeder Priester schaffe sich 12 Bürgen [dáfür], dass er Priesersatzung gesetzmässig halten wolle.
And let every priest find himself 12 sureties [for this], that he will keep the priests' law lawfully.
And each priest is to provide himself with 12 sureties, that he will rightly observe the priests’ law.
And every priest is to find for himself twelve bondsmen, to ensure that he will properly abide by the priests’ law.
div.note: Liebermann's German misprints ‘Priesersatzung’.; U: checked against Whitelock, EHD I (1979), and corrected (before: ‘And each priest is to provide himself with 12 sureties, that he will rightly observe the priest's law.’).

twelve bondsmen: This passage provides the only surviving attestation of the Old Norse–derived word festermen in Old English legislation. The use of such bondsmen is attested by a record in the York Gospels of the festermen who testified on behalf of an otherwise unidentified priest named Ælfric.

note.seg: Vgl. Gl Bürgschaft 4b. Die dort angeführte Urk. Ælfrics steht jetzt bei Björkman in Festschr. Morsbach 1; vgl. Beibl. z. Anglia 24 (1913) 281. Die festermen (ein Nord. Lehnwort von festumaðr, nicht erst in England komponiert) als Bürgen im anderen Sinne s. Gl Gewährbürge Z. 10; Grundbesitz 12a. Von derselben Wurzel lebt Nordenglisch noch fast ‘festbindend’, to fest(en), to fasten ‘bindend festmachen’, festen-(fasten-)penny ‘Angeld’; Wright Dial. diction. Flügel Engl. Dt. Wb kennt aus altem Recht fastingman ‘Bürge für das ruhige Verhalten eines Dritten’. Nichts zu tun hat das Wort mit den fastingmen in Urkk. 9. Jhs.—Die preostlagu scheint eben dies ganze Stück Northu zu meinen, identisch mit preosta lagu Insc²

Cf. Gl Bürgschaft 4b. The charter of Ælfric cited there is now printed by Björkman in Festschr. Morsbach 1; cf. Beibl. z. Anglia 24 (1913) 281. For the festermen (a Norse loanword from festumaðr, not first compounded in England) as sureties in another sense see Gl Gewährbürge l. 10; Grundbesitz 12a. From the same root Northern English still has fast ‘binding firmly’, to fest(en), to fasten ‘to make fast by binding’, festen-(fasten-)penny ‘earnest money’; Wright Dial. diction. Flügel Engl. Dt. Wb knows from old law fastingman ‘surety for the peaceable conduct of a third party’. The word has nothing to do with the fastingmen in charters of the 9th cent. — The preostlagu seems to mean precisely this whole section of Northu, identical with preosta lagu Insc²

note.seg: festermen. A list of 72 feslermen for a certain Æfric is entered on an end-leaf of the York Gospels, see Janet Cooper, “The list of Ælfric’s festermen in the York Gospels”, Yorks. Arch. journ., xlii (1969), 328–38.
